standard.title: Continuities and Changes in Australian Values and Identity
standard.description: continuities and changes in perspectives, responses, beliefs and values that have influenced the Australian way of life
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied continuities and changes in Australian society to Year 9 level, including shifting attitudes during the interwar period.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate continuities and changes in the perspectives, beliefs and values that have influenced the Australian way of life from the 1960s to the present.

nodes.label: Questioning traditional values in the 1960s–70s
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how events of the 1960s and 1970s led Australians to question traditional notions of egalitarianism, democracy, and national identity.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two events of the 1960s–70s that challenged traditional Australian values and explain how each produced questioning of those values.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate how Australians in the 1960s and 1970s, influenced by the events of those decades, began to question traditional notions of egalitarianism, a fair go, classlessness and democracy; analyse specific events: conscription and the Vietnam War (challenging the legitimacy of government military decisions), the Women's Liberation Movement (challenging gender roles and egalitarianism's gendered limits), and the dismissal of the Whitlam government (challenging democratic norms and constitutional conventions).
wider: Examine the Whitlam dismissal in depth as a constitutional crisis, analysing the competing interpretations of whether the Governor-General acted appropriately and what the event revealed about tensions in Australian democratic institutions
Compare the counterculture movements of the 1960s–70s in Australia with those in the USA and UK, examining how global social movements were adapted to the Australian context

response_modes.reason: The concept of 'continuity and change in values' is abstract. Ground it in the specific question: what did Australians believe before, what events challenged those beliefs, and what changed as a result? The Vietnam War and women's liberation are both well-evidenced cases for this analysis.

success_criteria: Identify at least two events of the 1960s–70s that challenged traditional Australian values
Explain how at least one of these events produced questioning of a specific Australian value (e.g. egalitarianism, democratic legitimacy)
Describe what 'traditional' Australian values — egalitarianism, a fair go, classlessness — meant in practice and why they came under challenge

nodes.label: Asia-Pacific engagement and religion
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare the Asia-Pacific engagement policies of different governments and examine the changing nature of religion in Australia.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare the Asia-Pacific engagement policies of at least two different governments and describe at least one change in Australian religious practice.
nodes.typical_width: Compare and contrast the Asia-Pacific engagement policies of Prime Minister Paul Keating (1991–1996) and Prime Minister John Howard (1996–2007) — examining their different visions for Australia's place in the Asia-Pacific region and the domestic debates each approach generated; examine the nature of religion in Australia — the changing attitudes to religious practice, the increase of non-Christian religions, and the growth of non-traditional Christian churches.
wider: Trace Australia's Asia-Pacific engagement across four governments (Whitlam, Fraser, Keating, Howard), evaluating whether the shifts represent genuine value change or strategic repositioning in response to changing circumstances

Investigate how the religious landscape of Australia changed as a result of post-war migration — examining how the arrival of Buddhist, Muslim, Hindu, and Sikh communities changed the religious composition of Australian society and how this was received

response_modes.reason: The Keating/Howard comparison is a productive case study in how political leadership shapes national identity. Widen it to include the religious diversity dimension — both are aspects of how Australian identity was contested and reshaped in the 1990s–2000s.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Keating/Howard contrast on Asia-Pacific engagement is a well-evidenced case for examining how political values shape foreign policy — and how the same strategic environment can be interpreted through fundamentally different value frameworks. It connects to K19's examination of Australia's international identity.
success_criteria: Compare the Asia-Pacific engagement policies of Keating and Howard, identifying at least two differences
Explain what each approach reveals about the values and priorities of the government that pursued it
Describe at least one change in Australian religious practice or composition since the post-war period
